stimulus.text:
“To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements, and the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities is sending ever-increasing multitudes to crowd them. The fifteen thousand tenant houses that were the despair of the sanitarian in the past generation have swelled into thirty-seven thousand, and more than twelve hundred thousand persons call them home.”

Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890), Introduction.
stimulus.source_note: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1890), Introduction. Public domain; text checked against Project Gutenberg eBook 45502.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stem: Riis links the growth of the tenements to “the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities.” That link best supports which claim?

options.text: Tenements were built mainly for wealthy families moving downtown
options.misconception: Puts wealthy families in housing Riis describes for the poor.

options.text: Migration into cities, from abroad and farms, outran the housing available
The federal government built the tenements to house new immigrants
options.misconception: Credits the government with building what private landlords built.

options.text: Immigrants preferred tenements to other kinds of housing
options.misconception: Treats crowded housing as a free choice.

rationales.A: Riis writes about the poor in tenements, not wealthy families moving downtown.
rationales.B: A drift of people into the cities that crowded ever more multitudes into tenements means the housing could not keep up with the migration.
rationales.C: Riis never says the government built the tenements. Private landlords built them for profit.
rationales.D: Riis describes crowding people were pushed into, not a housing choice they preferred.
rationales.general:
Join the drift to the crowding.
1. People drifted into the cities in ever-increasing multitudes.
2. Those multitudes crowded into the tenements.
3. Crowding that keeps growing means housing could not keep up.
4. The drift, not a preference for tenements, is what Riis blames.
Background: the books say the drift came from abroad and from farms, as machines cut farm labor.
Remember: when people outrun housing, crowding is the result, not the choice.
